title: Checkpoint capture of task state (foundational)
description: At safe points between stages, the manager serializes the full task state: completed stages, pending work items, and intermediate results. Checkpoints are written atomically, so a crash mid-write never leaves a half checkpoint that looks complete. The state is plain JSON, inspectable without special tooling. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
import json
state = {'stage': 2, 'done': ['crawl', 'index'], 'pending': ['rank'], 'results': {'hits': 42}}
blob = json.dumps(state)
print('checkpoint bytes:', len(blob))
print('restored stage:', json.loads(blob)['stage'])
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Session Continuity Manager practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Resume validation before restart (foundational)
description: Before resuming, the manager validates the checkpoint: schema check, checksum match, and a freshness test against the archive's current state. A checkpoint that fails validation is rejected outright rather than resumed into a corrupted task. Validation is what makes resume safe instead of merely convenient. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.

title: Progress restoration without redo (foundational)
description: On resume, completed stages are skipped and their cached intermediate results reloaded; only pending stages execute. The manager diffs the checkpoint's pending list against the plan to catch stages added since the checkpoint was written. This guarantees no work is repeated and no new work is silently dropped. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
plan = ['crawl', 'index', 'rank', 'report']
checkpoint_done = {'crawl', 'index'}
remaining = [s for s in plan if s not in checkpoint_done]
print('skipping completed:', sorted(checkpoint_done))
print('resuming with:', remaining)
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Session Continuity Manager practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Multi-device session handoff (foundational)
description: Checkpoints are stored server-side under a session token, so a task started on one device can resume on another by presenting the token. The handoff transfers state only, never credentials, and the token expires after use or a timeout. This makes long investigations portable across the user's devices. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
sessions = {}
def handoff(state):
    import secrets
    tok = secrets.token_hex(4)
    sessions[tok] = state
    return tok
tok = handoff({'stage': 3})
print('handoff token:', tok, '| resumes at stage', sessions[tok]['stage'])
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Session Continuity Manager practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Session expiry and cleanup (foundational)
description: Checkpoints expire after a configurable idle period, and expired sessions are deleted in a cleanup sweep. Expiry prevents stale state from being resumed into an archive that has moved on, which would produce subtly wrong results. The sweep logs what it removed so users can see that a session aged out. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
sessions = {'s1': datetime(2026, 10, 15), 's2': datetime(2026, 10, 21)}
now = datetime(2026, 10, 21, 12)
ttl = timedelta(days=3)
expired = [s for s, t in sessions.items() if now - t > ttl]
print('expired sessions cleaned:', expired)
